description: We're The Entangled Devs, a team of software developers and quantum-computing enthusiasts at NASA Space Apps Multan. For Lunar Landing Site Navigator, we're building an interactive planner to compare lunar sites using terrain, sunlight, and Earth-communication constraints, while exploring hybrid quantum-classical optimization with Qiskit. We welcome teammates skilled in lunar science, geospatial data, visualization, UI/UX, and research. Join us to turn NASA data into mission insights!
summary:
LunaPath is an interactive lunar mission-planning prototype developed by The Entangled Devs for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It addresses the challenge of selecting suitable lunar south-pole exploration locations by helping users examine sunlight availability and direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

Our application allows users to explore lunar locations, select mission dates, visualize Sun and Earth positions, compare visibility windows, and rank candidate locations using adjustable priorities. It features an interactive lunar south-pole explorer, visibility timelines, sky compass, custom site selection, terrain-horizon CSV integration, and downloadable analysis results.

LunaPath incorporates NASA's published Artemis III landing-region information and provides optional integration with NASA JPL Horizons for astronomical positioning data. Its offline demonstration mode is explicitly identified as illustrative rather than validated NASA ephemeris data.

By simplifying complex lunar planning concepts, LunaPath aims to support students, educators, researchers, and early-stage mission designers in understanding the trade-offs between solar power, Earth communication, and lunar exploration opportunities.
details:
LunaPath — Lunar South Pole Mission Opportunity Explorer

Team: The Entangled Devs
Local Event: Multan, Pakistan
Challenge: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

The Problem

Lunar south-pole exploration presents major scientific and engineering challenges. Extreme lighting conditions, permanently shadowed regions, complex terrain, and limited direct communication with Earth make choosing potential landing locations difficult.

Mission planners must consider when sunlight is available for solar power generation and when Earth is visible for communication. Although astronomical tools and scientific datasets exist, interpreting this information can be challenging for non-specialists.

Our Solution

We developed LunaPath, a web-based educational mission-planning application that simplifies the exploration and comparison of lunar south-pole locations.

LunaPath provides a unified interface where users can investigate how location and mission date influence sunlight and direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

Key Features

1. Interactive Lunar South-Pole Explorer

Users can explore a schematic south-pole map, select predefined reference locations such as Shackleton and de Gerlache, and add custom sites using lunar latitude and longitude coordinates.

2. Sunlight Visibility Analysis

The application visualizes solar elevation and estimates the proportion of sampled mission times when the Sun is above a selected horizon threshold.

3. Earth Communication Analysis

LunaPath examines Earth's elevation relative to the local horizon to identify possible direct-to-Earth visibility windows.

4. Mission-Date Selection

Users can choose a mission start date and analyze three-, seven-, or fourteen-day windows to investigate how conditions vary with time.

5. Site Comparison and Ranking

An adjustable scoring model combines sunlight and Earth-visibility opportunities to help users compare candidate locations according to their priorities.

6. Interactive Scientific Visualizations

The interface includes a lunar south-pole diagram, Sun and Earth elevation charts, a sky compass, visibility percentages, and comparative results.

7. Terrain-Horizon Integration

Users can import a CSV file containing terrain obstruction angles. This allows the application to consider a supplied local horizon rather than only assuming a flat geometric horizon. The included example terrain file is illustrative, not measured lunar topography.

8. NASA JPL Horizons Integration

An optional Python backend connects to NASA's JPL Horizons API to request astronomical positions of the Sun and Earth at selected lunar coordinates. Live retrieval requires an internet connection and successful API responses.

When NASA data is unavailable, the application offers an explicitly labeled offline analytical illustration.

9. Downloadable Reports

Users can export analysis results as JSON for documentation, comparison, and reproducibility.

Innovation and Creativity

LunaPath transforms complex astronomical visibility concepts into a clear, accessible mission-planning interface.

Our approach combines interactive visualization, transparent decision scoring, configurable terrain obstructions, and scientific data provenance.

We also explored a hybrid quantum-classical research direction using a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulation for selecting among candidate sites. The project includes a classical reference implementation and an optional Qiskit circuit experiment. This is an exploratory component and does not demonstrate quantum computational advantage.

Technologies Used

  • HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript for the interactive application
  • Python for the local server and NASA API integration
  • NASA JPL Horizons for optional live astronomical ephemerides
  • NASA Artemis III published landing-region information
  • SVG-based visualizations and graphical components
  • CSV data processing and JSON export
  • Optional Qiskit quantum-computing experiment

Scientific Methodology

The application compares the Sun's and Earth's elevation with the local horizon at sampled times throughout the selected mission period.

Sun visibility is determined using an adjustable minimum elevation threshold. Earth visibility is evaluated separately, and their overlap represents potential simultaneous sunlight and communication opportunities.

A transparent weighted scoring formula provides comparative rankings.

These calculations are intended for education and preliminary exploration, not certified landing-site selection.

Intended Impact

LunaPath can support students learning lunar exploration concepts, educators demonstrating scientific mission constraints, and early-stage researchers exploring how mission timing affects surface operations.

The longer-term vision is to integrate verified lunar terrain elevation models, more detailed power calculations, and improved communication analysis.

Current Limitations and Future Development

The current south-pole map is schematic rather than a verified terrain map. Offline Sun and Earth positions are simplified illustrations. Accurate terrain obstruction analysis requires independently validated terrain-horizon data, and the live NASA API integration requires external testing.

LunaPath does not currently assess landing hazards, spacecraft trajectories, or full communication link budgets.

Future development could incorporate NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter terrain datasets, validated terrain-horizon calculations, and more comprehensive mission feasibility models.

Conclusion

LunaPath makes the relationship between lunar geography, sunlight, communication, and mission timing easier to understand through a single interactive application.

Our goal is to make lunar exploration planning concepts more accessible while establishing a transparent foundation for future scientific and engineering improvements.
